stem: Why does the author call the make-up department of Gemini Studios an example of national integration? (40–50 words)
model_answer: The department brought together people from all over India long before the term was coined. It was first headed by a Bengali and then by a Maharashtrian, who was assisted by a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and several local Tamils — a miniature of the whole country working on one task.

model_answer: The office boy was a man of about forty who had joined the studios hoping to become a star, writer, director or lyricist. Instead he painted the faces of crowd players on crowd-shooting days. A bit of a poet, he felt his talent was wasted and blamed Kothamangalam Subbu, pouring his grievances into the author's ears.

label: PYQ-style
stem: What was the Moral Re-Armament Army, and what lasting influence did its visit leave on Tamil drama? (40–50 words)
hint: 1952, 200 people, anti-communist movement, two plays, sunrise–sunset sets.
model_answer: The Moral Re-Armament Army was an international group of about two hundred people from twenty nationalities, a counter-movement to communism, which visited Madras in 1952 and staged its plays at Gemini Studios. Though few understood its message, its simple sets and the sunrise and sunset scenes were copied by Tamil plays for years afterwards.

Influence: sunrise–sunset scenes in Tamil drama

label: PYQ-style
stem: Give a character sketch of Kothamangalam Subbu as presented in 'Poets and Pancakes'. (120–150 words)
hint: Position → loyalty → versatility in films → poet, novelist, actor → generosity → enemies → author's balanced irony.
model_answer:
Kothamangalam Subbu was officially a member of the Story Department but in practice the No. 2 at Gemini Studios. His greatest asset, the author says, was loyalty: he identified himself completely with the Boss and turned all his energy to the Boss's benefit.

He seemed born for films. Given a scene, he could suggest four ways of shooting it, and fourteen more if those were rejected; his inventiveness made filmmaking look easy. He was a poet who chose to write for the masses, a novelist whose Thillana Mohanambal created unforgettable characters, and a fine supporting actor who often outshone the lead. He was warm and generous, keeping a house full of relatives and friends he fed daily.

Yet such closeness to power made him enemies, and the frustrated office boy blamed him for every failure. Asokamitran draws him with admiration and a touch of irony — a gifted, loyal man whose success could not please everyone.

label: PYQ-style
stem: 'Poets and Pancakes' is marked by gentle humour and irony. Discuss with examples from the chapter. (120–150 words)
hint: Make-up makes people ugly; Clive's stables; national integration; office boy of forty; author's idle job; lawyer among poets; MRA sunsets; the poet nobody understood; the pavement book.
model_answer:
Asokamitran laughs quietly at the film world he knew from inside. The make-up department, housed in Robert Clive's old stables, exists to turn decent-looking people into crimson monsters; it is also, he notes solemnly, a model of national integration. The 'office boy' is a man of forty, a frustrated poet who paints crowd faces and blames Subbu for his wasted genius. The author's own job of cutting newspaper clippings looks so much like idleness that everyone feels free to advise him.

The irony sharpens with the legal adviser, a man of cold logic in pants and tie among khadi-clad dreamers, who ends an actress's career by simply recording her tantrum. The Moral Re-Armament Army comes to fight communism and is remembered for its sunrise and sunset scenes. Finally a famous English poet lectures a studio that cannot understand a word, and his identity is discovered years later in a book bought off the pavement.

The humour is never cruel; it comes from an affectionate eye for human absurdity.

scheme.step: Statement of tone; make-up room and national integration
Office boy, author's job, legal adviser — at least three instances
MRA sunsets; Spender unrecognised; book from the pavement
Conclusion on the nature of the humour; expression and length
